claim: Cotranslational assembly is widespread among protein complexes.
source: While recent evidence suggests that such cotranslational assembly is widespread, little is known about the properties of protein complexes associated with the phenomenon.
evidence: The manuscript cites recent evidence supporting this claim.

claim: Cotranslational assembly is particularly common between subunits that form large intermolecular interfaces.
source: Here, using a combination of proteome-specific protein complex structures and publicly available ribosome profiling data, we show that cotranslational assembly is particularly common between subunits that form large intermolecular interfaces.
evidence: The authors present their own analysis combining structural data with ribosome profiling data.

claim: Large interfaces have evolved as a means to maximize the chance of successful cotranslational subunit binding.
source: This strongly suggests that large interfaces have evolved as a means to maximise the chance of successful cotranslational subunit binding.
evidence: The authors infer this evolutionary interpretation from their data on interface size differences.

claim: The majority of proteins across all domains of life function as part of multimeric complexes.
source: The majority of proteins across all domains of life function as part of multimeric complexes.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the field.

claim: Ribosome profiling has laid down strong evidence that the assembly of protein complexes often starts on the ribosome.
source: To the present work, however, it is of outstanding relevance that ribosome profiling has laid down strong evidence that the assembly of protein complexes often starts on the ribosome (Duncan and Mata, 2011; Natan et al., 2017; Sepulveda et al., 2018; Shiber et al., 2018; Kamenova et al., 2019; Panasenko et al., 2019; Fujiwara et al., 2020; Bertolini et al., 2021; Seidel et al., 2022).
evidence: Multiple citations are provided supporting this claim.

claim: Two factors appear to be particularly important for cotranslational assembly: the proximity of nascent chains on adjacent or between juxtaposed ribosomes, and the localisation of interface residues towards the N-terminus of a protein.
source: Two factors appear to be particularly important for cotranslational assembly: the proximity of nascent chains on adjacent (cis) or between juxtaposed (trans) ribosomes, and the localisation of interface residues towards the N-terminus of a protein, which allows more time for an interaction to occur during translation (Shieh et al., 2015; Natan et al., 2018; Kamenova et al., 2019).
evidence: Citations are provided supporting these factors.

claim: Homomers frequently assemble on the same transcript via the interaction of adjacent elongating ribosomes.
source: Recent findings demonstrated that homomers, formed from multiple copies of a single type of polypeptide chain, frequently assemble on the same transcript via the interaction of adjacent elongating ribosomes (Bertolini et al., 2021).
evidence: A citation to Bertolini et al., 2021 supports this claim.

claim: Cotranslationally binding subunits have a tendency to fall out of solution or become degraded by orphan subunit surveillance mechanisms in the absence of their partner subunits.
source: It has been observed that cotranslationally binding subunits have a tendency to fall out of solution or become degraded by orphan subunit surveillance mechanisms in the absence of their partner subunits (Choe et al., 2016; Juszkiewicz and Hegde, 2018; Natan et al., 2018; Shiber et al., 2018; Kamenova et al., 2019).
evidence: Multiple citations support this observation.

claim: Interface size shows remarkable correspondence with subunit dissociation energy and is reflective of the evolutionary history of subunits within complexes.
source: Whilst the relationship between interface area and in vitro measured affinity is non-linear (Eisenberg and McLachlan, 1986; Horton and Lewis, 1992; Brooijmans et al., 2002; Vangone and Bonvin, 2015), interface area shows remarkable correspondence with subunit dissociation energy, and is reflective of the evolutionary history of subunits within complexes (Levy et al., 2008).
evidence: Citations support this claim about interface area properties.

claim: The size hierarchy of interfaces in protein complexes can be used to predict the order in which their subunits assemble, in good agreement with experimental data.
source: The size hierarchy of interfaces in protein complexes can be used to predict the order in which their subunits assemble, in good agreement with experimental data (Levy et al., 2008; Marsh et al., 2013; Wells et al., 2016).
evidence: Citations support this predictive capability.

claim: C2 symmetric subunits that assemble during translation expose 20% larger areas than those that do not.
source: In line with our expectation, C2 symmetric subunits that assemble during translation expose 20% larger areas than those that do not (Figure 1C; p = 7.2 × 10−7, Wilcoxon rank-sum test).
evidence: Statistical analysis of structural data is presented with p-value.

claim: Cotranslationally assembling cyclic homomers have interfaces that are 24% larger on average than those that do not assemble cotranslationally.
source: Despite the limited number of structures available, we detect a significant difference in interface area among soluble members of the cyclic symmetry group (Figure 1C), with the mean of cotranslationally forming subunits being 24% larger (p = 0.039, Wilcoxon rank-sum test).
evidence: Statistical analysis with p-value is provided.

claim: Cotranslationally assembling dihedral complexes have on average 33% larger interfaces than those assumed to assemble after their complete synthesis.
source: We find that cotranslationally assembling dihedral complexes have on average 33% larger interfaces than those assumed to assemble after their complete synthesis (Figure 1C; p = 1.6 × 10−6, Wilcoxon rank-sum test).
evidence: Statistical analysis with p-value is provided.

claim: Heterodimers that simultaneously assemble reveal a 15% larger interface area on average than those not detected to cotranslationally assemble.
source: When compared, heterodimers that simultaneously assemble reveal a 15% larger interface area on average than those not detected to cotranslationally assemble (Figure 1C; p = 7.9 × 10−3, Wilcoxon rank-sum test).
evidence: Statistical analysis with p-value is provided.

claim: N-terminal interfaces are significantly larger than C-terminal interfaces in cotranslationally assembling homodimers.
source: In fact, N-terminal interfaces are significantly larger than C-terminal interfaces in cotranslationally assembling homodimers (p = 0.021, Wilcoxon rank-sum test).
evidence: Statistical test result is provided.

claim: The difference in apolar interface area shows a stronger effect among homodimers than the total size.
source: We found that, while the difference in apolar interface area shows a stronger effect among homodimers than the total size (Wilcoxon effect size 0.24, p = 1.8 × 10−7, vs. 0.228, p = 7.2 × 10−7), the opposite is observed among heterodimers (Wilcoxon effect size 0.054, p = 0.262, vs. 0.127, p = 7.9 × 10−3).
evidence: Statistical comparison with effect sizes and p-values is provided.

claim: Cotranslationally assembling subunits have higher predicted affinities among both homo- and heterodimers.
source: As expected, this analysis revealed that cotranslationally assembling subunits have higher predicted affinities, or lower ΔG of binding (Figure 2D), among both homo- and heterodimers (Wilcoxon effect size, 0.166 for C2, p = 3.1 × 10−4, and 0.122 for heterodimers, p = 0.011), although these differences are also weaker than those observed with interface size.
evidence: Statistical analysis with effect sizes and p-values is provided.

claim: Cotranslationally assembling subunits possess a larger proportion of charged residues on the surface than other subunits.
source: We found significant differences in the NISc parameter between cotranslationally assembling and all other subunits among both homo- and heterodimers (Figure 2G), suggesting that cotranslationally assembling subunits possess a larger proportion of charged residues on the surface than other subunits.
evidence: Analysis of the NISc parameter is presented.

claim: Negatively charged amino acids in cotranslationally assembling subunits are overrepresented relative to other subunits.
source: We found that negatively charged amino acids in cotranslationally assembling subunits are overrepresented relative to other subunits (Figure 2H; Dunn's test of multiple comparisons, C2, p = 7.1 × 10−5 and heterodimers, p = 4.1 × 10−7), and we also detect a small but significant enrichment in positively charged amino acids, but only in homodimers (p = 6.0 × 10−3).
evidence: Statistical test results are provided.

claim: The net enrichment in charged amino acids on the surfaces of cotranslationally assembling heterodimeric subunits results in a lower isoelectric point than in other subunits.
source: This analysis revealed that the net enrichment in charged amino acids on the surfaces of cotranslationally assembling heterodimeric subunits results in a lower isoelectric point than in other subunits (Figure 2I; Wilcoxon rank-sum test, p = 9.1 × 10−5).
evidence: Statistical analysis of isoelectric points is provided.

claim: 281 interfaces on multi-interface heteromeric subunits may form in a simultaneous cotranslational fashion.
source: Using this method, we identified 281 interfaces on multi-interface heteromeric subunits that may form in a simultaneous cotranslational fashion.
evidence: The authors report the number of interfaces identified by their mapping method.

claim: Cotranslationally assembling interfaces are 19% larger than other interfaces on multi-interface heteromeric subunits.
source: Our results show that the identified cotranslationally assembling interfaces are indeed larger by 19% than other interfaces on these subunits (Figure 3B; p = 0.018, Wilcoxon signed-rank test).
evidence: Statistical analysis with p-value is provided.

claim: Simultaneously forming interfaces tend to form much earlier than other heteromeric interfaces in the complexes.
source: This analysis revealed that the identified interfaces tend to form much earlier than other heteromeric interfaces in the complexes (Figure 3C; p = 0.01, Wilcoxon signed-rank test).
evidence: Statistical analysis of assembly order is provided.

claim: A simultaneously forming interface is 1.7 times more likely to form early in the assembly pathway.
source: According to this, a simultaneously forming interface is 1.7 times more likely to form early (180 [67%] of 270 vs. 633 [54%] of 1171; p = 9.5 × 10−5, Fisher's exact test).
evidence: Statistical analysis with Fisher's exact test is provided.

claim: The average interface size of protein age groups is ordered almost perfectly according to evolutionary age for both human and yeast homo- and heteromers.
source: In Figure 4A, we show that the average interface size of the groups, for both human and yeast, is ordered almost perfectly according to evolutionary age of both homo- and heteromers.
evidence: Visual presentation of data showing the trend is provided.

claim: Older proteins with larger interfaces have a higher frequency of cotranslational assembly.
source: When we ask what percentage of each protein age group was found to assemble cotranslationally by Bertolini et al., 2021, there is a remarkable agreement between older proteins with larger interfaces having a higher frequency of cotranslational assembly (Figure 4B).
evidence: Analysis of cotranslational assembly frequency by protein age is presented.

claim: In E. coli, the first interface is larger than the last interface in 60% of cases.
source: The strongest effect is measured in E. coli, where the first interface is larger than the last interface in 60% of cases, and on average is 205 Å2 (15%) larger (p = 5.6 × 10−3, Wilcoxon signed-rank test).
evidence: Statistical analysis of E. coli interface sizes is provided.

claim: In humans, the first interface is larger than the last interface in 52% of cases, being 147 Å2 (13%) larger on average.
source: In humans, the trend is weaker, with the first interface larger in 52% of cases, being 147 Å2 (13%) larger on average (p = 0.022).
evidence: Statistical analysis of human interface sizes is provided.

claim: When using the 2000 Å2 filter, N-terminal interfaces are on average 23%, 31%, and 19% larger for E. coli, human, and yeast, respectively.
source: When using the 2000 Å2 filter, we observe that N-terminal interfaces are on average 23%, 31%, and 19% larger for E. coli, human, and yeast, respectively, significant for all.
evidence: Quantitative results from filtered analysis are provided.

claim: The size difference between the two interfaces is significantly larger in operon-encoded multi-interface heteromeric subunits, favouring the first interface.
source: In agreement with the above idea, we found that the size difference between the two interfaces is significantly larger in operon-encoded multi-interface heteromeric subunits, favouring the first interface (mean area difference of 317 Å2, p = 0.011).
evidence: Bootstrap analysis with p-value is provided.

claim: Removal of simultaneously assembling proteins increases the size difference between the first and the last translated interfaces from 13% to 18%.
source: Strikingly, removal of these proteins increases the size difference between the first and the last translated interfaces from 13% to 18% (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B; p = 0.014, Wilcoxon signed-rank test).
evidence: Statistical analysis comparing datasets is provided.

claim: Increasing the distance between the start points monotonically increases the extent of the area difference across all species.
source: Figure 5F shows the correlation between the separation of translation start points and the area differences of the first and the last interfaces (absolute values shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C). As expected, increasing the distance between the start points monotonically increases the extent of the area difference across all species.
evidence: Correlation analysis is presented in figures.

claim: Homomeric subunits are identical; therefore nascent chains are essentially colocalised by the nature of their synthesis.
source: This mechanism is highly effective because it takes advantage of the fact that homomeric subunits are identical; therefore nascent chains are essentially colocalised by the nature of their synthesis.
evidence: This is a logical inference about homomeric assembly.

claim: Heteromers can only employ the trans mode of assembly in eukaryotes, providing mechanisms that colocalise their transcripts exist.
source: On the other hand, heteromers, products of different genes that physically interact, can only employ the trans mode of assembly in eukaryotes, providing mechanisms that colocalise their transcripts exist (Liu et al., 2016b; Pizzinga et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2020; Chen and Mayr, 2022).
evidence: Citations support this claim about heteromeric assembly modes.

claim: Cotranslational assembly of heteromers may only require a single ribosome on each mRNA.
source: In contrast to homomers, cotranslational assembly of heteromers may only require a single ribosome on each mRNA, which could allow lowly abundant regulatory proteins to cotranslationally assemble (Heyer and Moore, 2016; Biever et al., 2020).
evidence: Citations support this claim about ribosome requirements.

claim: N-terminal interfaces are aggregation prone due to interference with cotranslational folding.
source: This observation may be explained under two assumptions: N-terminal interfaces are aggregation prone due to interference with cotranslational folding (Ciryam et al., 2013; Jacobs and Shakhnovich, 2017; Kudva et al., 2018; Kramer et al., 2019), and/or that cotranslationally forming interfaces possess unique structural properties that predispose them to aggregation in the absence of binding partners.
evidence: Citations support this assumption.

claim: Hydrophobicity remains the founding principle of protein–protein recognition theory.
source: Hydrophobic surfaces play a key role in nucleation theory (Hermann, 1972; Tanford, 1978; Chandler, 2005) and protein folding (Privalov and Khechinashvili, 1974; Chothia, 1975; Gething and Sambrook, 1992), but more importantly, hydrophobicity remains the founding principle of protein–protein recognition theory (Kauzmann, 1959; Chothia and Janin, 1975).
evidence: Citations support this principle.

claim: Interface size shows correspondence to hydrophobic area because larger interfaces contain more interface core residues.
source: Defined as the buried surface area between subunits, interface size shows correspondence to hydrophobic area because larger interfaces contain more interface core residues (Levy, 2010).
evidence: Citation supports this relationship.

claim: The relationship between interface area and in vitro measured affinity is non-linear.
source: Whilst the relationship between interface area and in vitro measured affinity is non-linear (Eisenberg and McLachlan, 1986; Horton and Lewis, 1992; Brooijmans et al., 2002; Vangone and Bonvin, 2015), interface area shows remarkable correspondence with subunit dissociation energy, and is reflective of the evolutionary history of subunits within complexes (Levy et al., 2008).
evidence: Citations support this claim about the non-linear relationship.

claim: The largest interfaces in a complex correspond to the earliest forming subcomplexes within the assembly pathway.
source: According to this theory, the largest interfaces in a complex correspond to the earliest forming subcomplexes within the assembly pathway, irrespective of the binding mode.
evidence: This is stated as a theory in the field.

claim: The trend in interface size is only significant and much larger in effect between N-terminally localised interfaces.
source: In all groups, there is a clear interface size trend wherein cotranslationally assembling subunits have a larger area. More interestingly, however, the trend is only significant and much larger in effect between N-terminally localised interfaces.
evidence: Analysis of interface location effects is presented.

claim: N-terminally localised interfaces are far more likely to represent cases of genuine cotranslational assembly.
source: One possible explanation for this is that N-terminally localised interfaces are far more likely to represent cases of genuine cotranslational assembly.
evidence: This is an inference from the data on interface location.

claim: Heteromeric interfaces are less hydrophobic than homomeric interfaces.
source: The origin of this sharp contrast is likely the fact that heteromeric interfaces are less hydrophobic (Jones and Thornton, 1996), and thus complexation is less likely to be primarily driven by the size of the hydrophobic patch of the interface.
evidence: Citation supports this claim about interface hydrophobicity.

claim: Interface size shows tremendous utility in discriminating cotranslationally assembling subunits because it is easily calculable and it is a fundamental property of protein–protein interactions.
source: Nevertheless, as demonstrated here, interface size shows tremendous utility in discriminating cotranslationally assembling subunits because it is easily calculable and it is a fundamental property of protein–protein interactions, unlike salt bridges or pi–pi interactions, which do not necessarily occur at every interface.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the analyses presented.

claim: Some subunits preferentially assemble cotranslationally with one partner, but not with a different partner from another complex.
source: Indeed, it has recently been shown among components of the nuclear pore complex that some subunits preferentially assemble cotranslationally with one partner, but not with a different partner from another complex (Seidel et al., 2022).
evidence: Citation supports this claim about selective cotranslational assembly.

claim: Cotranslational assembly may have been selected for because it increases the efficiency of assembly and avoids potentially damaging non-specific interactions.
source: Alternatively, cotranslational assembly may have been selected for, for example, because it increases the efficiency of assembly and avoids potentially damaging non-specific interactions.
evidence: This is presented as a hypothesis to be tested.

claim: Due to vectorial synthesis on the ribosome, N-terminal regions of proteins are more likely to be involved in binding events during translation.
source: Regardless of whether cotranslational assembly occurs simultaneously (Figure 1B) or sequentially (Figure 5A), due to vectorial synthesis on the ribosome, N-terminal regions of proteins are more likely to be involved in binding events during translation.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the mechanism of translation.

claim: If cotranslational assembly is adaptive, N-terminal interfaces in multi-interface heteromeric subunits should show a significant tendency to be larger than C-terminal interfaces.
source: Therefore, if cotranslational assembly is adaptive, we would expect that N-terminal interfaces in multi-interface heteromeric subunits, which will be translated first, should show a significant tendency to be larger than C-terminal interfaces, as illustrated in Figure 5B.
evidence: This is the hypothesis being tested.

claim: In E. coli, the first interface is on average 205 Å2 (15%) larger than the last interface.
source: The strongest effect is measured in E. coli, where the first interface is larger than the last interface in 60% of cases, and on average is 205 Å2 (15%) larger (p = 5.6 × 10−3, Wilcoxon signed-rank test).
evidence: Statistical analysis provides quantitative results.

claim: In yeast, the first interfaces are 130 Å2 (9%) larger on average, but the difference is not significant.
source: In yeast, although the first interfaces are 130 Å2 (9%) larger on average, the difference is not significant.
evidence: Statistical analysis shows non-significant result.

claim: Averaging over the three species, the first interface is larger than the last interface in 54% of multi-interface subunits.
source: Averaging over the three species, we observe first interface to be larger than the last interface in 54% of multi-interface subunits.
evidence: Summary statistic across species is provided.

claim: When considering multi-interface subunits of heteromeric complexes where at least one interface is >2000 Å2, the N-terminal interface is larger than the C-terminal interface nearly two thirds of the time.
source: Thus, when considering multi-interface subunits of heteromeric complexes where at least one interface is >2000 Å2, the N-terminal interface is larger than the C-terminal interface nearly two thirds of the time.
evidence: Summary of filtered analysis is provided.

claim: There has not been enough time for selection to considerably act on the assembly of younger subunits.
source: We hypothesise that this is because there has not been enough time for selection to considerably act on the assembly of these subunits, or because newer subunits tend to be required less for cotranslational interactions due their later assembly or functional roles they play.
evidence: This is a hypothesis to explain the observed data.

claim: Newer subunits tend to be required less for cotranslational interactions due to their later assembly or functional roles they play.
source: We hypothesise that this is because there has not been enough time for selection to considerably act on the assembly of these subunits, or because newer subunits tend to be required less for cotranslational interactions due their later assembly or functional roles they play.
evidence: This is a hypothesis to explain the observed data.

claim: In prokaryotes, many heteromeric complexes are encoded by operons.
source: Our attention was next drawn to E. coli, which demonstrated the strongest first versus last interface size trend. In prokaryotes, many heteromeric complexes are encoded by operons, where the different subunits are translated off of the same polycistronic mRNA molecules.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: Early studies in bacteria indicated that operon gene order is correlated to physical interactions between the encoded proteins.
source: Early studies in bacteria indicated that operon gene order is correlated to physical interactions between the encoded proteins (Mushegian and Koonin, 1996; Dandekar et al., 1998).
evidence: Citations support this claim.

claim: Cotranslational assembly is likely to be particularly common in operon-encoded heteromers.
source: Cotranslational assembly is likely to be particularly common in operon-encoded heteromers, given that the translation of different subunits is inherently colocalised.
evidence: This is an inference based on the mechanism of operon translation.

claim: The tendency for N-terminal interfaces to be larger should be stronger in operon-encoded E. coli heteromers, compared to those that are not operon encoded.
source: We hypothesised that the tendency for N-terminal interfaces to be larger should be stronger in operon-encoded E. coli heteromers, compared to those that are not operon encoded.
evidence: This is a hypothesis being tested.

claim: Purification of RecD is complicated by the formation of inclusion bodies, while the other two subunits remain in the soluble fraction.
source: One study reported that purification of RecD is complicated by the formation of inclusion bodies, while the other two subunits remain in the soluble fraction (Marsh and Teichmann, 2014).
evidence: Citation supports this experimental observation.

claim: A genetic analysis suggested that partially folded RecC and RecD might interact during translation, or that RecC forms a complex with RecB first, onto which RecD is then assembled.
source: Moreover, a genetic analysis suggested that partially folded RecC and RecD might interact during translation, or that RecC forms a complex with RecB first, onto which RecD is then assembled (Amundsen et al., 2002).
evidence: Citation supports this genetic analysis result.

claim: The first versus last interface trend may be the hallmark of sequential cotranslational assembly, rather than that of the simultaneous mode.
source: We speculate that the first versus last interface trend may be the hallmark of sequential cotranslational assembly (Figure 5A), rather than that of the simultaneous mode (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is speculation based on the data patterns.

claim: Simultaneous assembly is predominantly employed for the formation of homomeric protein complexes.
source: Bertolini et al., 2021 have suggested that simultaneous assembly is predominantly employed for the formation of homomeric protein complexes, which could mean sequential assembly is the more common cotranslational assembly mode in heteromers.
evidence: Citation supports this suggestion.

claim: The strong trend in E. coli supports the idea that sequential assembly is more common in heteromers.
source: The strong trend in E. coli also supports this idea, because polycistronic gene structure is more compatible with sequential cotranslational assembly (Shieh et al., 2015).
evidence: Citation and inference support this claim.

claim: In eukaryotes, large complexes and subunits of lowly abundant complexes may require an additional biological process to ensure their transcripts are colocalised for simultaneous assembly.
source: In eukaryotes, large complexes and subunits of lowly abundant complexes may require an additional biological process to ensure their transcripts are colocalised for simultaneous assembly and to facilitate further assembly steps (Keene, 2007; Chen and Mayr, 2022).
evidence: Citations support this claim.

claim: Sequential assembly may have evolved to exploit large interface areas for the recruitment of partner subunits.
source: Sequential assembly, on the other hand, may have evolved to exploit large interface areas for the recruitment of partner subunits.
evidence: This is an inference from the data.

claim: Five multi-interface heteromeric subunits in yeast that use the sequential assembly mode all follow the first versus last interface size trend.
source: Although a proteome-scale data set of cotranslationally assembling proteins is not available for yeast, we have identified case studies of five multi-interface heteromeric subunits in yeast that use the sequential assembly mode, and found that all five subunits follow the first versus last interface size trend (Table 1).
evidence: Case studies from literature are analyzed.

claim: Removal of simultaneously assembling proteins increases the size difference between the first and the last translated interfaces, suggesting enrichment in sequential assembly.
source: Strikingly, removal of these proteins increases the size difference between the first and the last translated interfaces from 13% to 18% (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B; p = 0.014, Wilcoxon signed-rank test). One explanation is that the remaining heteromers are enriched in sequential assembly, and thus exhibit a greater difference.
evidence: Statistical analysis and inference are provided.

claim: The later the translation of the last interface starts relative to the first, the higher the chance that assembly of the first interface will be undisturbed.
source: The later the translation of the last interface starts relative to the first, the higher the chance that assembly of the first interface will be undisturbed, free of competition with the partner subunit of the last interface.
evidence: This is a logical inference about assembly dynamics.

claim: The distance between translation start points of the first and last interfaces should correlate with the size difference in favour of the first interface.
source: Therefore, we hypothesised that the distance between translation start points of the first and last interfaces, which are the earliest emerged interface residues of each, should correlate with the size difference in favour of the first interface.
evidence: This is a hypothesis being tested.

claim: Increasing the distance between the start points monotonically increases the extent of the area difference across all species.
source: As expected, increasing the distance between the start points monotonically increases the extent of the area difference across all species.
evidence: Correlation analysis supports this claim.

claim: There is a pronounced preference in all species for a larger first interface when the separation is high.
source: In both subsets, there is a pronounced preference in all species for a larger first interface when the separation is high (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Analysis controlling for sequence length is provided.

claim: Interface area is important for assembly.
source: It has long been understood that interface area is important for assembly, but the capacity in which it shapes the hierarchy of individual interfaces on subunits remained elusive.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: The results demonstrate a strong correspondence between interface size and cotranslational subunit binding.
source: In this study, we first combined information from ribosome profiling with structural data on protein complexes to probe the importance of interface area in the process of cotranslational assembly. Our results demonstrate a strong correspondence between interface size and cotranslational subunit binding.
evidence: This is a summary of the study's findings.

claim: There is a clear trend across three evolutionarily distant species for the first translated interface of heteromeric subunits to be larger.
source: We found a clear trend across three evolutionarily distant species for the first translated interface of heteromeric subunits to be larger, suggesting that large interfaces have evolved to promote cotranslational assembly.
evidence: This is a summary of the study's findings.

claim: Cotranslational assembly may represent a ratchet-like mechanism of constructive neutral evolution.
source: While our results support the adaptive hypothesis of interface size, it is not entirely inconceivable that cotranslational assembly represents a ratchet-like mechanism of constructive neutral evolution (Gray et al., 2010; Hochberg et al., 2020), whereby a drift in interface properties creates ideal conditions for assembly on the ribosome.
evidence: This is presented as an alternative hypothesis with citations.

claim: Reversion to the post-translational route is prevented by the accumulation of mutations that are neutral in the subunit entrenched in cotranslational assembly, but would otherwise be deleterious in the ancestor.
source: Reversion to the post-translational route is prevented by the accumulation of mutations that are neutral in the subunit entrenched in cotranslational assembly, but would otherwise be deleterious in the ancestor.
evidence: This is a mechanistic explanation of neutral evolution.

claim: The strongest trend among E. coli heteromers is attributable to the widespread sequential assembly between mature subunits and nascent chains.
source: In light of current knowledge of bacterial operon structure and translation regulation, it is not surprising that we observed the strongest trend among E. coli heteromers with respect to the size of the interface that first emerges from the ribosome. Supposedly, the effect is attributable to the widespread sequential assembly between mature subunits and nascent chains, reflecting the mechanism of effective subunit recruitment by large N-terminal 'bait' interfaces.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the results.

claim: An interesting question for laboratory experiments is whether operon-encoded heteromers can assemble in the simultaneous mode.
source: An interesting question for laboratory experiments is whether operon-encoded heteromers can assemble in the simultaneous mode, providing that the structural organisation of the bacterial polysome allows for such a precise coordination (Brandt et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a question for future research.

claim: In homomers, large interfaces are more likely to form interactions before translation is complete because the subunits are localised to the same mRNA.
source: Its benefit in homomers for facilitating cotranslational assembly is clear, because the subunits are localised to the same mRNA, and large interfaces are more likely to form interactions before translation is complete.
evidence: This is a logical inference about homomeric assembly.

claim: One hypothesis argues the involvement of RNA-binding proteins that orchestrate transcript colocalisation in heteromers.
source: In heteromers, one hypothesis argues the involvement of RNA-binding proteins that orchestrate transcript colocalisation (Keene, 2007; Chen and Mayr, 2022), from where similar rules may apply to heteromer assembly as for homomers.
evidence: Citations support this hypothesis.

claim: Cotranslational assembly can result in transcript colocalisation, which is ablated when subunit affinity is decreased.
source: A more parsimonious hypothesis is formed on the observation that cotranslational assembly can result in transcript colocalisation, which is ablated when subunit affinity is decreased (Heidenreich et al., 2020).
evidence: Citation supports this observation.

claim: Affinity can play a role in the colocalisation of transcripts belonging to the same complex.
source: This may suggest that affinity, which correlates strongly though imperfectly with interface size (Brooijmans et al., 2002; Vangone and Bonvin, 2015), can play a role in the colocalisation of transcripts belonging to the same complex.
evidence: This is an inference based on cited correlations.

claim: Cotranslational assembly can be thought of as a hydrophobic collapse that shapes the quaternary structure of the complex.
source: Analogous to protein folding, cotranslational assembly can be thought of as a hydrophobic collapse that shapes the quaternary structure of the complex.
evidence: This is an analogy drawn by the authors.

claim: A wide array of ribosome-associated chaperones are vital for nascent chain homeostasis.
source: As with folding in the cell, the involvement of other factors must not be overlooked. A wide array of ribosome-associated chaperones are vital for nascent chain homeostasis (Oh et al., 2011; Döring et al., 2017; Koldewey et al., 2017; Shiber et al., 2018) and the degree to which they choreograph assembly steps is yet to be elucidated.
evidence: Citations support this claim.

claim: The degree to which ribosome-associated chaperones choreograph assembly steps is yet to be elucidated.
source: A wide array of ribosome-associated chaperones are vital for nascent chain homeostasis (Oh et al., 2011; Döring et al., 2017; Koldewey et al., 2017; Shiber et al., 2018) and the degree to which they choreograph assembly steps is yet to be elucidated.
evidence: This identifies a gap in current knowledge.

claim: Cotranslational assembly should make the dominant-negative effect less common in homomers because it can limit the mixing that occurs between wild-type and mutant subunits.
source: Interestingly, cotranslational assembly should actually make the dominant-negative effect less common in homomers, because it can limit the mixing that occurs between wild-type and mutant subunits.
evidence: This is a logical inference about genetic effects.

claim: It remains to be seen whether dominant-negative mutations are in fact less common in cotranslationally assembling complexes.
source: It remains to be seen whether dominant-negative mutations are in fact less common in cotranslationally assembling complexes.
evidence: This identifies a question for future research.

claim: Evolutionary selection against N-terminal interface contacts to avoid premature assembly was previously found in homomers.
